title: Is there a friend for life
titleChinese: 是否存在一辈子的朋友？
paragraphs: Who do you count as your friends? From our BFF to a work mate, it’s good to have someone to chew the fat with or offer comfort and support. But when it comes to friendship, is it more important to have quantity or quality?

The recent isolation we have endured due to the coronavirus pandemic has made some of us question our friendships. We’ve fallen out of touch with friends and acquaintances, and it may feel awkward, but do we actually have to rekindle every relationship we once had? It might be time to take stock and think about who you kept in touch with, who you missed talking to, and who you didn’t. In short, maybe it’s time to reset your list of real mates.

There’s no obligation to stay friends, and writing for BBC Worklife, Bryan Lufkin says: “While people have known for years that friendships are unquestionably good for your health, experts say it’s only natural for acquaintances and even friends to fall by the wayside as time goes on – and it’s nothing to feel guilty about.”

Of course, it can be hard to choose who’s in your friendship circle. This is what Suzanne Degges-White, professor of counselling at Northern Illinois University, calls our ‘friendscape’. She says, “in life, as we go through certain stages and ages, our attention shifts, and we want to be around people who are like us.”

So, changing friends is normal, but we still need those special pals who’ve known us long term. These are friendships we invest time in. According to Robin Dunbar, a professor of evolutionary psychology at the University of Oxford, these are your inner circle of friends – your “shoulders to cry on” – and you have to see them at least once a week to keep them in that circle. He adds that the friends that do drift are mostly “friendships of convenience”. But the advice for maintaining a good friendship is to share how you feel with someone you trust – this can help strengthen your friendship as well as giving you both a chance to support each other.

vocabulary.entry: BFF /ˌbiː ef ˈef/ n. 最好的朋友（全称best friend forever）
vocabulary.example: She has been my BFF since we were in primary school.
vocabulary.translation: 她从小学起就是我最好的朋友。

vocabulary.entry: work mate /ˈwɜːk meɪt/ n. 同事；工友
vocabulary.example: My work mate helped me finish the difficult task on time.
vocabulary.translation: 我的同事帮我按时完成了这项艰巨的任务。

vocabulary.entry: chew the fat /tʃuː ðə fæt/ 闲聊；侃大山
vocabulary.example: We often chew the fat over a cup of coffee after work.
vocabulary.translation: 下班后我们经常喝着咖啡闲聊。

vocabulary.entry: quantity /ˈkwɒntəti/ n. 数量；数目
vocabulary.example: Quality is more important than quantity when it comes to choosing friends.
vocabulary.translation: 择友时，质量比数量更重要。

vocabulary.entry: quality /ˈkwɒləti/ n. 质量；品质
vocabulary.example: The watch is cheap, but its quality is surprisingly good.
vocabulary.translation: 这块手表价格便宜，但质量却出奇地好。

vocabulary.entry: isolation /ˌaɪsəˈleɪʃn/ n. 隔离；孤立

vocabulary.translation: 长时间的隔离让她更加珍惜社交互动。

vocabulary.entry: endure /ɪnˈdjʊə(r)/ v. 忍受；忍耐

vocabulary.translation: 事故后她不得不忍受巨大的痛苦。

vocabulary.entry: fall out of touch with /fɔːl aʊt əv tʌtʃ wɪð/ 与……失去联系
vocabulary.example: I fell out of touch with my childhood friend after moving to another city.
vocabulary.translation: 搬到另一个城市后，我就和儿时的朋友失去了联系。

vocabulary.entry: acquaintance /əˈkweɪntəns/ n. 熟人；相识的人

vocabulary.translation: 他只是个熟人，不是我的密友。

vocabulary.entry: awkward /ˈɔːkwəd/ adj. 令人尴尬的；不自在的
vocabulary.example: It was awkward when we met each other after the argument.
vocabulary.translation: 争吵后我们碰面，场面很尴尬。

vocabulary.entry: rekindle /ˌriːˈkɪndl/ v. 重新点燃；恢复（关系）
vocabulary.example: They tried to rekindle their friendship after years of separation.
vocabulary.translation: 多年分离后，他们试图恢复往日的友谊。

vocabulary.entry: take stock /teɪk stɒk/ 评估；审视
vocabulary.example: It's time to take stock of your life and set new goals.
vocabulary.translation: 是时候审视你的人生并设定新目标了。

vocabulary.entry: reset /ˌriːˈset/ v. 重置；重新设定
vocabulary.example: She decided to reset her priorities and spend more time with family.
vocabulary.translation: 她决定重新设定自己的优先事项，花更多时间陪伴家人。

vocabulary.entry: mate /meɪt/ n. 朋友；伙伴

vocabulary.translation: 我大学时的老朋友这周末要来看我。

vocabulary.translation: 你没有义务接受这份邀请。

vocabulary.translation: 她对工作的投入无疑令人钦佩。

vocabulary.entry: counselling /ˈkaʊnsəlɪŋ/ n. 咨询；辅导

vocabulary.translation: 公众舆论已转向支持这项新政策。

vocabulary.translation: 投入时间和精力维护良好的友谊很重要。

vocabulary.translation: 进化心理学研究人类行为是如何随时间演变的。

vocabulary.translation: 他们曾经是亲密的朋友，但毕业后就渐渐疏远了。

vocabulary.entry: friendships of convenience /ˈfrendʃɪps əv kənˈviːniəns/ 功利性友谊；因便利而建立的友谊

vocabulary.example: Regular communication is key to maintaining a healthy friendship.
vocabulary.translation: 定期沟通是维持健康友谊的关键。

title: Should boredom be boring
paragraphs: How bored are you? Having nothing to do, or doing the same task again and again, can certainly be demotivating. And if boredom persists, you can lose your lust for life, and it can even affect your mental health. But does being bored have to be boring?

A lack of stimulation can lead to boredom – this is when we start to yawn and our mind wanders. It can happen at home or at school, but it’s at work where some experts think being chronically bored can have damaging consequences. This situation has been termed ‘boreout’ and is the opposite of ‘burnout’. Writing for BBC Worklife, Bryan Lufkin says this happens “when we are bored by our work to the point that we feel it is totally meaningless. Our job seems pointless, our tasks devoid of value.” It can be caused by working in a demoralising physical environment or feeling under-challenged. Studies show depression from boreout can affect workers outside the office and lead to physical ailments from insomnia to headaches. But Bryan adds that “being able to identify it in us, is critical for tackling it.”

When it becomes mind-numbing and extreme, some people joke about ‘dying of boredom’. According to Luis Villazon, writing for the Science Focus website, boredom is just a state of mind which won’t kill you, though it can depress the immune system in some people. He says “The greatest risk from boredom stems from the things you do to combat it. People who are easily bored are more likely to engage in dangerous sports [...]”, for example. But some experts say boredom is a natural thing and it should be seen in a more positive light. If we see it as an opportunity, it could ignite our creativity. And if our boredom is at work, it could force us to engage with mentors, career counsellors or even our bosses. And Lotta Harju from EM Lyon Business School told the BBC, “boreout can mark a transition into something else: a different career entirely, or a different role in the organisation. If people only take its cue.”

vocabulary.entry: demotivating /ˌdiːˈməʊtɪveɪtɪŋ/ adj. 使人泄气的；降低积极性的
vocabulary.example: Repetitive tasks can be demotivating for most employees.
vocabulary.translation: 重复性的工作对大多数员工来说会让人泄气。

vocabulary.entry: persist /pəˈsɪst/ v. 持续；延续
vocabulary.example: If the pain persists, you should consult a doctor immediately.
vocabulary.translation: 如果疼痛持续不退，你应该立即去看医生。

vocabulary.entry: lust for life /lʌst fɔː laɪf/ 对生活的热爱；生命的热忱
vocabulary.example: Her energy and lust for life are truly inspiring to everyone around her.
vocabulary.translation: 她的活力和对生活的热爱，真正鼓舞着身边的每一个人。

vocabulary.entry: stimulation /ˌstɪmjuˈleɪʃn/ n. 刺激；激发
vocabulary.example: Children need plenty of mental stimulation to develop their intelligence.
vocabulary.translation: 儿童需要充足的智力刺激来开发他们的智慧。

vocabulary.entry: wander /ˈwɒndə(r)/ v. （思绪）走神；漫游
vocabulary.example: My mind tends to wander when I'm listening to long lectures.
vocabulary.translation: 听冗长的讲座时，我的思绪很容易走神。

vocabulary.entry: chronically /ˈkrɒnɪkli/ adv. 长期地；慢性地
vocabulary.example: The region has been chronically affected by water shortages for years.
vocabulary.translation: 这个地区多年来长期受到水资源短缺的影响。

vocabulary.entry: boreout /ˈbɔːraʊt/ n. 职场无聊倦怠症
vocabulary.example: Boreout often occurs when employees are given tasks with no real purpose.
vocabulary.translation: 当员工被分配到毫无实际意义的任务时，职场无聊倦怠症就很容易发生。

vocabulary.entry: burnout /ˈbɜːnaʊt/ n. 职业倦怠；精疲力竭
vocabulary.example: Many teachers suffer from burnout due to heavy workloads and stress.
vocabulary.translation: 许多教师因繁重的工作量和压力而患上职业倦怠症。

vocabulary.entry: meaningless /ˈmiːnɪŋləs/ adj. 无意义的；空洞的
vocabulary.example: He found his job meaningless and decided to quit and pursue his dream.
vocabulary.translation: 他觉得自己的工作毫无意义，决定辞职去追求梦想。

vocabulary.entry: pointless /ˈpɔɪntləs/ adj. 无意义的；徒劳的
vocabulary.example: It's pointless to argue with him because he never changes his mind.
vocabulary.translation: 和他争论是徒劳的，因为他从不改变主意。

vocabulary.entry: devoid of /dɪˈvɔɪd əv/ 缺乏；没有
vocabulary.example: The room was devoid of any furniture, making it look empty and cold.
vocabulary.translation: 这个房间里一件家具都没有，看起来空旷又冷清。

vocabulary.entry: demoralising /dɪˈmɒrəlaɪzɪŋ/ adj. 令人泄气的；使士气低落的
vocabulary.example: Constant criticism from his boss was demoralising for the young employee.
vocabulary.translation: 老板的不断批评让这位年轻员工感到士气低落。

vocabulary.entry: under-challenged /ˌʌndəˈtʃælɪndʒd/ adj. 未受到足够挑战的；大材小用的
vocabulary.example: Talented employees often feel under-challenged in rigid work environments.
vocabulary.translation: 有才华的员工在刻板的工作环境中常常感到大材小用。

vocabulary.entry: ailment /ˈeɪlmənt/ n. 小病；疾病
vocabulary.example: The herbal tea is said to relieve common ailments like colds and headaches.
vocabulary.translation: 这种花草茶据说能缓解感冒、头痛之类的常见小病。

vocabulary.entry: insomnia /ɪnˈsɒmniə/ n. 失眠；失眠症
vocabulary.example: Stress and anxiety are the main causes of insomnia in many adults.
vocabulary.translation: 压力和焦虑是许多成年人失眠的主要原因。

vocabulary.entry: mind-numbing /ˈmaɪnd nʌmɪŋ/ adj. 令人麻木的；使人昏昏欲睡的
vocabulary.example: The mind-numbing routine of his job made him eager for a change.
vocabulary.translation: 这份工作单调得让人麻木，让他迫切想要做出改变。

vocabulary.entry: die of boredom /daɪ ɒv ˈbɔːdəm/ 无聊到极点
vocabulary.example: I thought I would die of boredom waiting for the delayed train for two hours.
vocabulary.translation: 等晚点的火车等了两个小时，我觉得自己都要无聊死了。

vocabulary.entry: depress /dɪˈpres/ v. 降低；抑制；使沮丧
vocabulary.example: Poor diet and lack of exercise can depress the body's immune system.
vocabulary.translation: 不良饮食和缺乏运动可能会抑制人体的免疫系统。

vocabulary.entry: immune system /ɪˈmjuːn ˈsɪstəm/ 免疫系统
vocabulary.example: Eating plenty of fruits and vegetables helps boost your immune system.
vocabulary.translation: 多吃水果和蔬菜有助于增强你的免疫系统。

vocabulary.entry: combat /ˈkɒmbæt/ v. 对抗；应对
vocabulary.example: The government has launched a new campaign to combat air pollution.
vocabulary.translation: 政府发起了一项新的运动来对抗空气污染。

vocabulary.entry: in a positive light /ɪn ə ˈpɒzətɪv laɪt/ 从积极的角度；以正面的眼光
vocabulary.example: We should try to look at this difficult situation in a positive light.
vocabulary.translation: 我们应该试着从积极的角度看待这个困境。

vocabulary.entry: ignite /ɪɡˈnaɪt/ v. 点燃；激起；引发
vocabulary.example: The teacher's inspiring words ignited the students' interest in science.
vocabulary.translation: 老师鼓舞人心的话语激发了学生们对科学的兴趣。

vocabulary.entry: creativity /ˌkriːeɪˈtɪvəti/ n. 创造力；创造性
vocabulary.example: The workshop is designed to encourage creativity and innovation among participants.
vocabulary.translation: 这个工作坊旨在鼓励参与者发挥创造力和创新精神。

vocabulary.entry: mentor /ˈmentɔː(r)/ n. 导师；指导者
vocabulary.example: She was lucky to have a wise mentor who guided her through her early career.
vocabulary.translation: 她很幸运，有一位睿智的导师在她职业生涯初期指导她。

vocabulary.entry: career counsellor /kəˈrɪə ˈkaʊnsələ(r)/ 职业顾问
vocabulary.example: A career counsellor can help you figure out your strengths and suitable job paths.
vocabulary.translation: 职业顾问可以帮你认清自己的优势和适合的职业发展道路。

vocabulary.entry: transition /trænˈzɪʃn/ n. 过渡；转变
vocabulary.example: The transition from student life to working life can be challenging for many young people.
vocabulary.translation: 从学生生活过渡到职场生活，对许多年轻人来说可能充满挑战。

vocabulary.entry: take its cue /teɪk ɪts kjuː/ 领会暗示；按提示行事
vocabulary.example: The team took its cue from the manager and changed their strategy immediately.
vocabulary.translation: 团队领会了经理的暗示，立即调整了策略。

sentences.english: How bored are you?
sentences.chinese: 你有多无聊？

sentences.english: Having nothing to do, or doing the same task again and again, can certainly be demotivating.
sentences.chinese: 无所事事，或是反复做同一项任务，无疑会让人提不起劲。

sentences.english: And if boredom persists, you can lose your lust for life, and it can even affect your mental health.
sentences.chinese: 如果无聊感持续不散，你可能会失去对生活的热情，甚至还会影响心理健康。

sentences.english: But does being bored have to be boring?
sentences.chinese: 但无聊就一定得是乏味的吗？

sentences.english: A lack of stimulation can lead to boredom – this is when we start to yawn and our mind wanders.
sentences.chinese: 缺乏刺激会引发无聊——这时我们会开始打哈欠，思绪也会飘忽不定。

sentences.english: It can happen at home or at school, but it’s at work where some experts think being chronically bored can have damaging consequences.
sentences.chinese: 这种情况可能发生在家里或学校，但一些专家认为，在职场中，长期的无聊会带来破坏性的后果。

sentences.english: This situation has been termed ‘boreout’ and is the opposite of ‘burnout’.
sentences.chinese: 这种状态被称为“职业无聊症”，是“职业倦怠症”的对立面。

sentences.english: Writing for BBC Worklife, Bryan Lufkin says this happens “when we are bored by our work to the point that we feel it is totally meaningless.
sentences.chinese: 布莱恩·勒夫金在为BBC职场生活频道撰稿时表示，这种情况的发生是“当我们对工作感到极度无聊，以至于觉得工作完全没有意义。

sentences.english: Our job seems pointless, our tasks devoid of value.”
sentences.chinese: 我们的工作似乎毫无价值，手头的任务也毫无价值。”

sentences.english: It can be caused by working in a demoralising physical environment or feeling under-challenged.
sentences.chinese: 造成这种状态的原因可能是身处令人萎靡的工作环境，或是感觉工作缺乏挑战性。

sentences.english: Studies show depression from boreout can affect workers outside the office and lead to physical ailments from insomnia to headaches.
sentences.chinese: 研究表明，由职业无聊症引发的抑郁情绪，会影响员工的日常生活，还会导致从失眠到头痛等一系列身体疾病。

sentences.english: But Bryan adds that “being able to identify it in us, is critical for tackling it.”
sentences.chinese: 但布莱恩补充道：“能够意识到自己正处于这种状态，是解决问题的关键。”

sentences.english: When it becomes mind-numbing and extreme, some people joke about ‘dying of boredom’.
sentences.chinese: 当无聊变得令人麻木且极端时，有些人会开玩笑说“无聊得要死”。

sentences.english: According to Luis Villazon, writing for the Science Focus website, boredom is just a state of mind which won’t kill you, though it can depress the immune system in some people.
sentences.chinese: 路易斯·维拉松在为《科学焦点》网站撰稿时表示，无聊只是一种精神状态，并不会置人于死地，不过它可能会降低一些人的免疫力。

sentences.english: He says “The greatest risk from boredom stems from the things you do to combat it.
sentences.chinese: 他说：“无聊带来的最大风险，源于人们为了排解无聊而做出的举动。

sentences.english: People who are easily bored are more likely to engage in dangerous sports [...]”, for example.
sentences.chinese: 例如，容易感到无聊的人更有可能参与危险的运动……

sentences.english: But some experts say boredom is a natural thing and it should be seen in a more positive light.
sentences.chinese: ”但一些专家认为，无聊是一种很自然的现象，我们应该从更积极的角度看待它。

sentences.english: If we see it as an opportunity, it could ignite our creativity.
sentences.chinese: 如果我们把它视为一种机遇，它可能会激发我们的创造力。

sentences.english: And if our boredom is at work, it could force us to engage with mentors, career counsellors or even our bosses.
sentences.chinese: 而如果这种无聊感源于工作，它可能会促使我们主动寻求导师、职业顾问甚至上司的帮助。

sentences.english: And Lotta Harju from EM Lyon Business School told the BBC, “boreout can mark a transition into something else: a different career entirely, or a different role in the organisation.
sentences.chinese: 里昂商学院的洛塔·哈尔尤在接受BBC采访时表示：“职业无聊症可能标志着一种转变的开端：要么彻底转行，要么在公司内部换一个不同的岗位。

sentences.english: If people only take its cue.”
sentences.chinese: 前提是如果人们愿意听从它发出的信号。”

title: A teddy bear for life
titleChinese: 为什么大人也爱泰迪熊？
paragraphs: One thing we always remember from our childhood is our favourite teddy bear. This soft, ragged toy was our comfort and companion. As we grow up, we normally give up our childish ways, and our furry friend often ends up in storage or at a jumble sale. But that’s not the case for everyone.

It seems that some grown-ups continue to need their cuddly toy by their sides. One sleep survey suggested a tenth of people in the UK need a teddy bear in bed. And for some adults, soft toys remain an essential presence – they take them wherever they go.

A cuddly toy can come in many forms – animals, strange shapes or just a piece of stuffed material. But it’s the teddy bear in particular that seems to have an enduring appeal – it gives us a nostalgic feeling and a reminder of our younger days. Writing for the BBC, historian David Cannadine says, “Perhaps it’s that bears represent the happy security of a childhood friend who never changes or lets you down.” For whatever reason, teddies appeal to both children and adults of all ages.

The teddy bear is much celebrated these days, and they’ve become something that we don’t just grow up with – people buy them as adults too. There are shops which sell only teddy bears, there are teddy bear museums in many countries, and teddy bear festivals regularly take place around the world.

While our soft toys offer us a kind of comfort blanket, some experts say it’s nothing to be ashamed of. It’s sometimes good to let go of the constraints of adult life and be a big kid again. And research commissioned by Barclaycard in the UK found 44% of adults have purchased playthings they enjoyed as children because they bring back happy memories. Colouring books, cuddly toys and board games were top of the list. So, if you’re still keeping your teddy a secret, don’t worry – you’re not alone!

title: Why should we take a shower
paragraphs: Bath or shower? How do you prefer to keep yourself clean? Whatever your daily ablutions, we know it’s important to have good personal hygiene. Nobody wants to smell, and nobody wants to catch your odour! A shower can bring you certain other benefits, but how often should we wash ourselves under a watery spray?

Although you might think taking a daily shower should be part of your cleaning ritual, there’s no hard and fast rule, although dermatologists agree that as a society, we shower too often. In fact, too much washing can deplete the vital oils in our skin. It can waste water as well. However, if you have a fitness regime that causes you to sweat, a more regular sprinkle of water is recommended to stop you ponging!

How often you shower is, of course, a personal choice. There’s nothing better than a hot, soapy scrub under the shower, and this doesn’t just have to be to clean yourself. Some people enjoy a shower to help them relax, warm up or to soothe any aches and pains. It’s also a good opportunity to wash your hair at the same time. Again, though, experts say we shouldn’t shower too often because, like your skin, your hair contains essential oils that you don’t want to lose through excessive scrubbing.

If the idea of a hot, steaming shower appeals, how about a freezing cold one instead? This might be a necessity if your boiler has broken, but some people choose this option because it has many health benefits, some experts claim. There is increasing evidence that braving an icy shower in the morning could keep illness at bay and may even help your brain stay sharp. A BBC podcast called Just One Thing with Michael Mosley, found the shock of being doused with cold water could have a positive impact on your body and brain.
The thought of a cold shower might not make you jump out of bed in the morning, but whatever the temperature, a splash of water will wake you up and make you feel and smell great!

vocabulary.entry: ablution /əˈbluːʃn/ n. 洗漱；沐浴（常用复数形式ablutions）

vocabulary.entry: personal hygiene /ˈpɜːsənl ˈhaɪdʒiːn/ 个人卫生

vocabulary.translation: 良好的个人卫生对预防疾病传播至关重要。

vocabulary.entry: odour /ˈəʊdə(r)/ n. 气味；臭味
vocabulary.example: The unpleasant odour from the bin made the room uncomfortable to stay in.
vocabulary.translation: 垃圾桶里散发的难闻气味让这个房间待着很不舒服。

vocabulary.entry: watery spray /ˈwɔːtəri spreɪ/ 水花喷淋

vocabulary.entry: ritual /ˈrɪtʃuəl/ n. 例行公事；习惯做法

vocabulary.translation: 关于一个人需要多少睡眠，并没有硬性规定。

vocabulary.entry: dermatologist /ˌdɜːməˈtɒlədʒɪst/ n. 皮肤科医生

vocabulary.translation: 上周我就皮肤过敏的问题咨询了皮肤科医生。

vocabulary.entry: deplete /dɪˈpliːt/ v. 耗尽；使枯竭

vocabulary.translation: 过度使用这些产品会耗尽头发中的天然油脂。

vocabulary.entry: vital oil /ˈvaɪtl ɔɪl/ 必需油脂

vocabulary.translation: 皮肤表面的必需油脂有助于保持肌肤水润。

vocabulary.entry: fitness regime /ˈfɪtnəs reɪˈʒiːm/ 健身计划

vocabulary.translation: 运动后彻底用肥皂擦洗可以去除污垢和汗水。

vocabulary.entry: soothe /suːð/ v. 缓解；抚慰
vocabulary.example: The warm bath helped to soothe her sore muscles after hiking.
vocabulary.translation: 温水浴帮助缓解了她徒步后酸痛的肌肉。

vocabulary.entry: ache and pain /eɪk ənd peɪn/ 各种疼痛
vocabulary.example: Hot compresses can ease the aches and pains caused by cold weather.
vocabulary.translation: 热敷可以缓解寒冷天气带来的各种疼痛。

vocabulary.entry: excessive /ɪkˈsesɪv/ adj. 过多的；过分的
vocabulary.example: Excessive use of air conditioning can dry out your skin.
vocabulary.translation: 过度使用空调会让你的皮肤变得干燥。

vocabulary.entry: steaming /ˈstiːmɪŋ/ adj. 冒蒸汽的；热气腾腾的

vocabulary.translation: 寒冷的早晨，她走进热气腾腾的淋浴间取暖。

vocabulary.entry: freezing cold /ˈfriːzɪŋ kəʊld/ 极冷的；冰冷的

sentences.english: Bath or shower?

sentences.english: How do you prefer to keep yourself clean?

sentences.english: Whatever your daily ablutions, we know it’s important to have good personal hygiene.

sentences.english: Some people enjoy a shower to help them relax, warm up or to soothe any aches and pains.

sentences.english: It’s also a good opportunity to wash your hair at the same time.

sentences.english: Again, though, experts say we shouldn’t shower too often because, like your skin, your hair contains essential oils that you don’t want to lose through excessive scrubbing.
sentences.chinese: 不过专家同样提醒，洗头不宜过于频繁，因为和皮肤一样，头发中也含有不可或缺的油脂，过度清洗会导致这些油脂流失。

sentences.english: If the idea of a hot, steaming shower appeals, how about a freezing cold one instead?
sentences.chinese: 如果热气腾腾的热水澡合你心意，那要不要试试冰爽的冷水澡呢？

sentences.english: This might be a necessity if your boiler has broken, but some people choose this option because it has many health benefits, some experts claim.
sentences.chinese: 如果家里的热水器坏了，冷水澡就可能是不可避免的选择，但有专家称，有些人会主动选择冷水澡，因为它对健康大有裨益。

sentences.english: There is increasing evidence that braving an icy shower in the morning could keep illness at bay and may even help your brain stay sharp.
sentences.chinese: 越来越多的证据表明，早上勇敢地冲个冷水澡，不仅能预防疾病，甚至还能帮助保持大脑思维敏捷。

sentences.english: A BBC podcast called Just One Thing with Michael Mosley, found the shock of being doused with cold water could have a positive impact on your body and brain.
sentences.chinese: 迈克尔·莫斯利主持的BBC播客《一件小事》发现，身体被冷水浇透时的那种冲击感，会对身心产生积极影响。

sentences.english: The thought of a cold shower might not make you jump out of bed in the morning, but whatever the temperature, a splash of water will wake you up and make you feel and smell great!
sentences.chinese: 想到早上要冲冷水澡，你可能对于起床这件事兴致缺缺，但无论水温冷热，冲个澡都能让你神清气爽，不仅体感舒适，身上还会香香的！

title: Stay-at-home fathers“
titleChinese: 全职奶爸”不再是非主流
paragraphs: There aren’t many parents who would say that raising children is easy. For many people, having children can force parents to choose between career and family. Sometimes it comes down to finances – sending a child to nursery or hiring a nanny can be a huge financial burden that is unsustainable, while others may feel it’s better to be a hands-on parent. These days, more and more men are choosing to stay at home to look after their offspring. So why are more dads opting to put their careers on hold, and what does the job entail?

With more women working outside the home than 70 years ago, if the need is there for one parent to stay at home, it could simply come down to who earns more – the biggest breadwinner. And with attitudes changing towards a man’s role in the family, it seems to be easier for them to enter full-time parenthood. Sadly, though, men may still face stigmas by choosing to raise their child. A 2013 study in the US by the Pews Research Center found that 51% of people thought children were better off if a mother is home and doesn’t have a job, while 8% say the same about a father. But what do parents have to do when they choose to stay with their kids?

In the early stages, a baby is totally dependent on a carer. The changing of nappies, burping after milk and making sure they feed on time are just some of the vital 24-7 activities an infant relies on. During this period, many parents take paternity and maternity leave from work. But as a child gets older, it can become less about necessity and more about choice. Rather than opt for a creche, which can prove expensive, either parent may remain at home to educate, protect and play with their child to help them develop and grow.

It’s a difficult job, with a demanding ‘boss’, but it can also be incredibly rewarding for those willing to do it. And with attitudes changing towards who should stay at home, maybe more and more fathers will choose to become stay-at-home dads.

title: What is road rage
paragraphs: We all know driving can be stressful. One minute you’re minding your own business and the next someone cuts you up. Manoeuvres like that can be annoying and irritating, but for some of us, it can make us incandescent with rage. So what is road rage, and what things can cause it?

Road rage, simply put, is a sudden burst of anger that motorists experience when they feel angered by something another driver, cyclist or pedestrian has done. Road rage can manifest itself in several ways, including verbal or physical threats, insults, and even dangerous driving. The drivers themselves may feel anxiety and stress, which can cause them to speed or swerve across the road. Experts like Leon James, a professor of traffic psychology at the University of Hawaii, US, warn that experiencing these moments, especially repeatedly, could be harmful to our health due to the number of stress hormones entering our bodies.

So, what can cause us to experience road rage? Being tailgated, undertaken on a busy motorway, seeing someone swooping across several lanes, chatting on their phone, or hogging the middle lane in front of us are just some of the things that may stress us. And what about parking? Someone stealing the space we wanted at the last second could tip us over the edge! Being aware of what can trigger these feelings of rage may be key to controlling it.

So what can we do to keep relaxed? Try driving in a good mood, and if you see a traffic jam, just remember that they can’t be avoided. And try leaving a little earlier in future. Also, if you see someone who is really angry, try not to maintain eye contact, and don’t get out of the car to confront them. And if you feel stressed and anxious, try pulling over somewhere and resting while you calm down.
So the next time you feel stressed while driving, just remember road rage can happen to anyone – and relaxing a bit when you feel that way may not just make it safer for you, but for others too.

vocabulary.entry: cut up /kʌt ʌp/ （车辆）突然超车抢道

vocabulary.entry: road rage /rəʊd reɪdʒ/ 路怒症；公路暴怒
vocabulary.example: Road rage incidents have increased significantly in urban areas in recent years.
vocabulary.translation: 近年来，城市地区的路怒症事件明显增多。

vocabulary.entry: simply put /ˈsɪmpli pʊt/ 简而言之；简单地说
vocabulary.example: Simply put, we need to reduce costs to keep the business running.
vocabulary.translation: 简而言之，我们需要降低成本来维持业务运转。

vocabulary.entry: burst of anger /bɜːst ɒv ˈæŋɡə(r)/ 一阵怒火；突发的愤怒
vocabulary.example: She had a sudden burst of anger when she heard the unfair decision.
vocabulary.translation: 听到这个不公的决定时，她突然怒火中烧。

vocabulary.entry: motorist /ˈməʊtərɪst/ n. 驾车者；机动车驾驶员
vocabulary.example: The sign is designed to alert motorists to the upcoming roadworks.
vocabulary.translation: 这个标识是用来提醒驾车者前方有道路施工。

vocabulary.entry: cyclist /ˈsaɪklɪst/ n. 骑自行车的人
vocabulary.example: Cyclists should always wear helmets for their own safety.
vocabulary.translation: 骑自行车的人为了自身安全应该始终佩戴头盔。

vocabulary.entry: pedestrian /pəˈdestriən/ n. 行人
vocabulary.example: Drivers must give way to pedestrians at zebra crossings.
vocabulary.translation: 司机在斑马线处必须礼让行人。

vocabulary.entry: manifest itself /ˈmænɪfest ɪtˈself/ 显现；表现出来
vocabulary.example: Symptoms of the illness usually manifest themselves within a few days.
vocabulary.translation: 这种疾病的症状通常会在几天内显现出来。

vocabulary.entry: verbal threat /ˈvɜːbl θret/ 言语威胁
vocabulary.example: The man was arrested for making verbal threats to his neighbour.
vocabulary.translation: 这名男子因对邻居进行言语威胁而被逮捕。

vocabulary.entry: physical threat /ˈfɪzɪkl θret/ 人身威胁
vocabulary.example: The security guard intervened to stop the physical threat against the customer.
vocabulary.translation: 保安介入制止了针对顾客的人身威胁。

vocabulary.entry: insult /ˈɪnsʌlt/ n. 侮辱；冒犯
vocabulary.example: She couldn't tolerate the insult and walked out of the room immediately.
vocabulary.translation: 她无法忍受这种侮辱，立刻走出了房间。

vocabulary.entry: dangerous driving /ˈdeɪndʒərəs ˈdraɪvɪŋ/ 危险驾驶
vocabulary.example: Dangerous driving can lead to serious accidents and even fatalities.
vocabulary.translation: 危险驾驶可能导致严重事故甚至死亡。

vocabulary.entry: swerve /swɜːv/ v. （车辆）突然转向；急转弯
vocabulary.example: The driver had to swerve to avoid hitting the stray dog.
vocabulary.translation: 司机不得不急转弯以避免撞到那只流浪狗。

vocabulary.entry: traffic psychology /ˈtræfɪk saɪˈkɒlədʒi/ 交通心理学
vocabulary.example: Traffic psychology studies the behaviour of drivers and pedestrians on the road.
vocabulary.translation: 交通心理学研究道路上驾车者和行人的行为。

vocabulary.entry: stress hormone /stres ˈhɔːməʊn/ 压力荷尔蒙
vocabulary.example: Cortisol is a common stress hormone released when people feel anxious.
vocabulary.translation: 皮质醇是人们感到焦虑时释放的一种常见压力荷尔蒙。

vocabulary.entry: tailgate /ˈteɪlɡeɪt/ v. 跟车过近；追尾行驶
vocabulary.example: It's dangerous to tailgate other vehicles, especially in bad weather.
vocabulary.translation: 跟车过近很危险，尤其是在恶劣天气下。

vocabulary.entry: undertake /ˌʌndəˈteɪk/ v. （在高速公路上）从内侧车道超车
vocabulary.example: In the UK, it is illegal to undertake on most motorways.
vocabulary.translation: 在英国，大多数高速公路上从内侧车道超车是违法的。

vocabulary.entry: motorway /ˈməʊtəweɪ/ n. 高速公路
vocabulary.example: We took the motorway to get to the airport faster.
vocabulary.translation: 我们走高速公路，以便更快到达机场。

vocabulary.entry: swoop across /swuːp əˈkrɒs/ 猛地横穿（道路）
vocabulary.example: The bird swooped across the road, causing the driver to brake suddenly.
vocabulary.translation: 那只鸟猛地横穿马路，导致司机紧急刹车。

vocabulary.entry: lane /leɪn/ n. （道路的）车道
vocabulary.example: The slow vehicle should keep to the left-hand lane on the motorway.
vocabulary.translation: 低速车辆在高速公路上应靠左行驶。

vocabulary.entry: hog the middle lane /hɒɡ ðə ˈmɪdl leɪn/ 霸占中间车道
vocabulary.example: Many drivers dislike those who hog the middle lane without overtaking.
vocabulary.translation: 很多司机讨厌那些霸占中间车道却不超车的人。

vocabulary.entry: tip sb over the edge /tɪp ˈsʌmbədi ˈəʊvə ði edʒ/ 使某人忍无可忍；让某人情绪失控
vocabulary.example: The long wait and the rude staff finally tipped her over the edge.
vocabulary.translation: 漫长的等待和粗鲁的工作人员终于让她忍无可忍。

vocabulary.entry: trigger /ˈtrɪɡə(r)/ v. 引发；触发
vocabulary.example: Lack of sleep can trigger headaches in some people.
vocabulary.translation: 睡眠不足会引发一些人头痛。

vocabulary.entry: traffic jam /ˈtræfɪk dʒæm/ 交通堵塞
vocabulary.example: We were stuck in a traffic jam for two hours on our way to the concert.
vocabulary.translation: 我们去音乐会的路上堵了两个小时的车。

vocabulary.entry: maintain eye contact /meɪnˈteɪn aɪ ˈkɒntækt/ 保持眼神交流
vocabulary.example: It's polite to maintain eye contact when talking to someone.
vocabulary.translation: 与人交谈时保持眼神交流是礼貌的做法。

vocabulary.entry: confront /kənˈfrʌnt/ v. 对峙；对抗
vocabulary.example: He decided not to confront the angry driver to avoid a conflict.
vocabulary.translation: 为了避免冲突，他决定不与那个愤怒的司机对峙。

vocabulary.entry: pull over /pʊl ˈəʊvə(r)/ 把车停到路边
vocabulary.example: The police officer asked the driver to pull over for a routine check.
vocabulary.translation: 警察要求司机把车停到路边接受例行检查。

sentences.english: We all know driving can be stressful.
sentences.chinese: 我们都知道开车是件很有压力的事。

sentences.english: One minute you’re minding your own business and the next someone cuts you up.
sentences.chinese: 前一秒你还在正常行驶，下一秒就有人突然强行加塞。

sentences.english: Manoeuvres like that can be annoying and irritating, but for some of us, it can make us incandescent with rage.
sentences.chinese: 这样的驾驶操作着实令人心烦气恼，对有些人来说，甚至会让他们怒火中烧。

sentences.english: So what is road rage, and what things can cause it?
sentences.chinese: 那么，什么是路怒症？又有哪些因素会引发路怒症呢？

sentences.english: Road rage, simply put, is a sudden burst of anger that motorists experience when they feel angered by something another driver, cyclist or pedestrian has done.
sentences.chinese: 简单来说，路怒症是驾驶人因受到其他司机、骑行者或行人的行为刺激，而产生的突发性暴怒情绪。

sentences.english: Road rage can manifest itself in several ways, including verbal or physical threats, insults, and even dangerous driving.
sentences.chinese: 路怒症的表现形式多种多样，包括言语或肢体威胁、辱骂，甚至是危险驾驶行为。

sentences.english: The drivers themselves may feel anxiety and stress, which can cause them to speed or swerve across the road.
sentences.chinese: 产生路怒情绪的司机自身也会感到焦虑和紧张，进而可能出现超速行驶或突然变道等行为。

sentences.english: Experts like Leon James, a professor of traffic psychology at the University of Hawaii, US, warn that experiencing these moments, especially repeatedly, could be harmful to our health due to the number of stress hormones entering our bodies.
sentences.chinese: 美国夏威夷大学交通心理学教授利昂·詹姆斯等专家提醒，这类情绪爆发的时刻，尤其是反复出现时，会使大量压力荷尔蒙进入人体，对健康造成损害。

sentences.english: So, what can cause us to experience road rage?
sentences.chinese: 那么，哪些情况会引发路怒症呢？

sentences.english: Being tailgated, undertaken on a busy motorway, seeing someone swooping across several lanes, chatting on their phone, or hogging the middle lane in front of us are just some of the things that may stress us.
sentences.chinese: 被后车跟车过近、在繁忙的高速公路上被从内侧车道超车、看到有人突然连续变道、开车时打电话，或是有人长时间霸占中间车道行驶，这些都可能让我们感到烦躁。

sentences.english: And what about parking?
sentences.chinese: 停车时的情况呢？

sentences.english: Someone stealing the space we wanted at the last second could tip us over the edge!
sentences.chinese: 就在你准备停车的最后一刻，有人抢了你的车位，这足以让你情绪失控！

sentences.english: Being aware of what can trigger these feelings of rage may be key to controlling it.
sentences.chinese: 了解哪些因素会触发愤怒情绪，或许是控制路怒症的关键。

sentences.english: So what can we do to keep relaxed?
sentences.chinese: 那么，我们该如何保持放松的心态呢？

sentences.english: Try driving in a good mood, and if you see a traffic jam, just remember that they can’t be avoided.
sentences.chinese: 尽量带着好心情开车，如果遇到交通堵塞，要记住这是不可避免的情况。

sentences.english: And try leaving a little earlier in future.
sentences.chinese: 以后可以试着早点出门。

sentences.english: Also, if you see someone who is really angry, try not to maintain eye contact, and don’t get out of the car to confront them.
sentences.chinese: 此外，如果看到有人怒气冲冲，尽量不要和对方对视，也不要下车对峙。

sentences.english: And if you feel stressed and anxious, try pulling over somewhere and resting while you calm down.
sentences.chinese: 如果你自己感到紧张焦虑，尝试把车停在安全的地方，休息一下，平复情绪。

sentences.english: So the next time you feel stressed while driving, just remember road rage can happen to anyone – and relaxing a bit when you feel that way may not just make it safer for you, but for others too.
sentences.chinese: 所以下次开车感到压力时，请记住，任何人都可能患上路怒症。当你感到烦躁时，试着放松一点，这不仅能让你自己更安全，也能为他人带来安全。

title: When neighbours go wrong
titleChinese: 造成邻里不和的种种因素
paragraphs: Do you know the names of the people who live next door? Chances are you live next to someone, but do you actually know them? Sadly, the only time we do seem to hear about people’s neighbours is when things go wrong – hearing people say things like they have the neighbours from hell! So, what does go wrong?

When talking about famous feuds with people who live in proximity, you only need to think of the Montagues and Capulets in Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet. Thankfully, most real-life quarrels don’t go that far. These days, especially in cities, many people live in condominiums, tightly packed into apartment blocks. Our neighbours are all around us – so what issues can come from that?

The first obvious cause of dispute is noise pollution. Loud bass pumping through the walls, construction, or people arguing next door can disrupt the harmony of your living space. Asking someone directly to turn the music down can cause you to feel anxious. However, getting someone like a building manager involved to speak to your neighbour and making complaints official can make things more awkward down the line as you didn’t speak to your neighbour directly.

And then what about smells? If your neighbour likes eating especially pungent food, something that offends your nostrils, and that smell drifts through your window, what can you do? Some other common issues include water leaking through the ceiling, pets making noise, and littering from the balcony above you.

And then, if you’re lucky enough to own a garden, that can present even more issues to fight with your neighbour about! This could include hedges and fences that are too high, balls and toys invading your garden or hitting your windows, and boundary disputes over where your neighbours’ land ends. All these can create animosity over time.

It’s not easy living next door to someone, especially if they’re noisy. But having a clear and honest line of dialogue might help. Also, try considering if the things you are doing could upset your neighbours. If it’s something that would upset you, maybe think again.

vocabulary.entry: neighbours from hell /ˈneɪbəz frəm hel/ （口语）地狱邻居；令人头疼的邻居
vocabulary.example: She moved out quickly because she had neighbours from hell who partied every night.
vocabulary.translation: 她很快就搬走了，因为她的邻居特别糟心，每晚都开派对。

vocabulary.entry: feud /fjuːd/ n. 长期不和；世仇
vocabulary.example: The two families have been in a feud for over a hundred years.
vocabulary.translation: 这两大家族的世仇已经持续了一百多年。

vocabulary.entry: in proximity /ɪn prɒkˈsɪməti/ 在附近；邻近
vocabulary.example: The new hospital was built in proximity to the residential area.
vocabulary.translation: 这家新医院建在了居民区附近。

vocabulary.entry: quarrel /ˈkwɒrəl/ n. 争吵；口角
vocabulary.example: The trivial matter led to a bitter quarrel between the two friends.
vocabulary.translation: 这件小事引发了两个朋友之间激烈的争吵。

vocabulary.entry: condominium /ˌkɒndəˈmɪniəm/ n. 公寓大楼；共管公寓
vocabulary.example: He bought a spacious apartment in a new condominium downtown.
vocabulary.translation: 他在市中心一栋新建的公寓大楼里买了一套宽敞的公寓。

vocabulary.entry: tightly packed /ˈtaɪtli pækt/ 拥挤的；紧密排列的
vocabulary.example: The tightly packed audience filled every seat in the theatre.
vocabulary.translation: 拥挤的观众坐满了剧院里的每一个座位。

vocabulary.entry: apartment block /əˈpɑːtmənt blɒk/ 公寓楼
vocabulary.example: They live on the fifth floor of a modern apartment block.
vocabulary.translation: 他们住在一栋现代化公寓楼的五楼。

vocabulary.entry: dispute /dɪˈspjuːt/ n. 争端；争执
vocabulary.example: The two countries held talks to resolve the border dispute.
vocabulary.translation: 两国举行会谈，以解决边境争端。

vocabulary.entry: noise pollution /nɔɪz pəˈluːʃn/ 噪音污染
vocabulary.example: The government has introduced laws to control noise pollution in cities.
vocabulary.translation: 政府出台了相关法律来控制城市里的噪音污染。

vocabulary.entry: loud bass /laʊd beɪs/ 重低音
vocabulary.example: The loud bass from the party next door kept me awake all night.
vocabulary.translation: 隔壁派对的重低音吵得我整夜没睡。

vocabulary.entry: disrupt harmony /dɪsˈrʌpt ˈhɑːməni/ 破坏和谐
vocabulary.example: The constant arguments between the couple disrupted the harmony of the neighbourhood.
vocabulary.translation: 这对夫妻频繁的争吵破坏了邻里间的和谐。

vocabulary.entry: building manager /ˈbɪldɪŋ ˈmænɪdʒə(r)/ 物业经理；大楼管理员
vocabulary.example: I reported the broken lift to the building manager this morning.
vocabulary.translation: 今天早上我向物业经理报修了故障电梯。

vocabulary.entry: pungent /ˈpʌndʒənt/ adj. 气味刺鼻的；辛辣的
vocabulary.example: The pungent smell of garlic filled the kitchen.
vocabulary.translation: 厨房里弥漫着大蒜刺鼻的气味。

vocabulary.entry: offend nostrils /əˈfend ˈnɒstrɪlz/ 刺鼻；让鼻子不适
vocabulary.example: The smell of rotten eggs offended our nostrils as we walked past the bin.
vocabulary.translation: 我们路过垃圾桶时，腐烂鸡蛋的气味刺鼻难忍。

vocabulary.entry: water leaking /ˈwɔːtə ˈliːkɪŋ/ 漏水
vocabulary.example: Water leaking from the ceiling damaged the carpet in the living room.
vocabulary.translation: 天花板漏水损坏了客厅的地毯。

vocabulary.entry: littering /ˈlɪtərɪŋ/ n. 乱扔垃圾
vocabulary.example: Littering in public places is punishable by fine in this city.
vocabulary.translation: 在这座城市，公共场所乱扔垃圾会被处以罚款。

vocabulary.entry: balcony /ˈbælkəni/ n. 阳台
vocabulary.example: She likes to sit on the balcony and read books on sunny afternoons.
vocabulary.translation: 她喜欢在晴朗的午后坐在阳台上看书。

vocabulary.entry: hedge /hedʒ/ n. 树篱；绿篱
vocabulary.example: The gardener trimmed the hedge to keep it neat and tidy.
vocabulary.translation: 园丁修剪了树篱，让它保持整齐美观。

vocabulary.entry: fence /fens/ n. 栅栏；篱笆
vocabulary.example: They built a wooden fence around the garden to keep the dog inside.
vocabulary.translation: 他们在花园周围建了一道木栅栏，防止狗跑出去。

vocabulary.entry: boundary dispute /ˈbaʊndri dɪˈspjuːt/ 边界纠纷
vocabulary.example: The boundary dispute between the two farmers was settled by a local official.
vocabulary.translation: 当地官员调解解决了两位农民之间的边界纠纷。

vocabulary.entry: animosity /ˌænɪˈmɒsəti/ n. 敌意；怨恨
vocabulary.example: Years of argument have created a lot of animosity between the two families.
vocabulary.translation: 多年的争吵让两家人之间积怨颇深。

vocabulary.entry: line of dialogue /laɪn əv ˈdaɪəlɒɡ/ 沟通渠道；对话途径
vocabulary.example: Establishing a clear line of dialogue is key to solving the problem.
vocabulary.translation: 建立清晰的沟通渠道是解决这个问题的关键。

vocabulary.entry: invade /ɪnˈveɪd/ v. 侵入；闯入
vocabulary.example: The children's balls often invade our garden from the next door.
vocabulary.translation: 邻居家孩子的球经常会滚进我们的花园。

vocabulary.entry: construction /kənˈstrʌkʃn/ n. 建筑施工
vocabulary.example: The construction outside the window made it hard to concentrate on work.
vocabulary.translation: 窗外的建筑施工噪音让人难以专心工作。

vocabulary.entry: official complaint /əˈfɪʃl kəmˈpleɪnt/ 正式投诉
vocabulary.example: He filed an official complaint with the property management about the noise issue.
vocabulary.translation: 他就噪音问题向物业提交了正式投诉。

sentences.english: Do you know the names of the people who live next door?
sentences.chinese: 你知道隔壁邻居的名字吗？

sentences.english: Chances are you live next to someone, but do you actually know them?
sentences.chinese: 你大概率有邻居，但你真的了解他们吗？

sentences.english: Sadly, the only time we do seem to hear about people’s neighbours is when things go wrong – hearing people say things like they have the neighbours from hell!
sentences.chinese: 遗憾的是，我们似乎只有在邻里关系出问题的时候，才会听到人们谈论邻居——比如常听到有人抱怨自己遇上了“极品邻居”！

sentences.english: So, what does go wrong?
sentences.chinese: 那么，究竟是哪些问题会引发邻里矛盾呢？

sentences.english: When talking about famous feuds with people who live in proximity, you only need to think of the Montagues and Capulets in Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet.
sentences.chinese: 说到著名的邻里宿怨，你只需要想想莎士比亚《罗密欧与朱丽叶》中的蒙太古家族和凯普莱特家族就够了。

sentences.english: Thankfully, most real-life quarrels don’t go that far.
sentences.chinese: 幸好，现实生活中的大多数邻里争吵都不会闹到那么过分。

sentences.english: These days, especially in cities, many people live in condominiums, tightly packed into apartment blocks.
sentences.chinese: 如今，尤其是在城市里，许多人住在格局紧凑的公寓楼里。

sentences.english: Our neighbours are all around us – so what issues can come from that?
sentences.chinese: 邻居们近在咫尺——那么，这种居住环境会引发哪些问题呢？

sentences.english: The first obvious cause of dispute is noise pollution.
sentences.chinese: 引发邻里纠纷的第一个显而易见的原因是噪音污染。

sentences.english: Loud bass pumping through the walls, construction, or people arguing next door can disrupt the harmony of your living space.
sentences.chinese: 穿墙而来的强劲低音、施工的嘈杂声、或是隔壁邻居的争吵声，都可能破坏你居住空间的和谐氛围。

sentences.english: Asking someone directly to turn the music down can cause you to feel anxious.
sentences.chinese: 直接要求对方把音乐声调小，可能会让你感到紧张不安。

sentences.english: However, getting someone like a building manager involved to speak to your neighbour and making complaints official can make things more awkward down the line as you didn’t speak to your neighbour directly.
sentences.chinese: 但如果让物业经理这类人出面沟通，或是正式投诉，又会因为你没有直接和邻居交涉，而让后续的邻里相处变得更加尴尬。

sentences.english: And then what about smells?
sentences.chinese: 还有气味问题。

sentences.english: If your neighbour likes eating especially pungent food, something that offends your nostrils, and that smell drifts through your window, what can you do?
sentences.chinese: 如果你的邻居喜欢吃气味特别浓烈、让你难以忍受的食物，而且这些味道飘进了你的窗户，你该怎么办？

sentences.english: Some other common issues include water leaking through the ceiling, pets making noise, and littering from the balcony above you.

sentences.english: And then, if you’re lucky enough to own a garden, that can present even more issues to fight with your neighbour about!
sentences.chinese: 如果你足够幸运，拥有一片自家花园，那可能会引发更多和邻居争吵的问题！

sentences.english: This could include hedges and fences that are too high, balls and toys invading your garden or hitting your windows, and boundary disputes over where your neighbours’ land ends.
sentences.chinese: 比如邻居家的树篱或围栏过高、球和玩具掉进你家花园甚至砸到窗户、以及关于邻里地界划分的纠纷。

sentences.english: All these can create animosity over time.
sentences.chinese: 久而久之，这些问题都会滋生邻里间的敌意。

sentences.english: It’s not easy living next door to someone, especially if they’re noisy.

sentences.english: But having a clear and honest line of dialogue might help.

sentences.english: Also, try considering if the things you are doing could upset your neighbours.
sentences.chinese: 此外，不妨换位思考一下，自己的所作所为是否会打扰到邻居。

sentences.english: If it’s something that would upset you, maybe think again.
sentences.chinese: 如果换作是你，也会为此感到不快，那或许就该三思而后行了。

title: The benefits of boxing
paragraphs: Boxing has been practised for centuries – it was even one of the sports in the original Olympic Games in ancient Greece. More recently, boxing has become mainstream in the UK, with hundreds of thousands of people from all walks of life participating in the sport every week. But why? The answer lies in the physical, mental and even social benefits boxing can bring.

Its physical benefits are clear. Whether it’s practising with a punching bag, sparring with a partner or facing an opponent in the ring, boxing can be an intense form of exercise and give a full-body workout. It can improve muscular strength, and it can also increase anaerobic fitness – allowing someone to work out harder, for longer. These can, in turn, have a positive impact on other aspects of physical well-being, like heart health and weight management.

But the high physical demands of the sport aren’t just good for the body – boxing can also have a positive impact on someone’s mental well-being. Dr Jessica Pinchbeck, Senior Lecturer in Sport and Fitness at the Open University, says that boxing ‘can alleviate some of the symptoms of anxiety and depression’. Exercising regularly is already widely known to be good for mental health, but boxing can also bring a sense of discipline and focus.

And there is a third benefit to putting on the boxing gloves. Practising punches can be done alone, of course, but boxing is not just an individual activity – it also involves working with others to train and stay safe. Dr Gavin Williams, Senior Lecturer in Education at the Open University, says that this cooperation and teamwork can ‘create a sense of identity… and belonging’. So, no matter what the reason that attracts someone to boxing, the interactive elements of the sport, mean it can also have profound social benefits.
Good for body, mind and social interactions? It’s not surprising that more and more people are stepping into the ring.

title: Why camping can be so much fun
paragraphs: When you go on holiday, where do you like to stay? Do you like the luxury of a five-star hotel, the convenience of a self-catering apartment or do you prefer the freedom of sleeping under canvas? If you haven’t tried the latter, maybe you should join the increasing number of people who are enjoying the simple pleasures of camping.

By grabbing your tent, and some additional accessories, it’s easy to head off to the countryside and enjoy a night or two under the stars. Many campers are ditching the trappings of their modern, hectic life to do this, encouraged by experts who say a few peaceful nights in the middle of nowhere might be a good way to unwind and improve our sleep patterns and well-being. It is also, of course, a good low-budget holiday option.

For the adventurous, wild camping is the ultimate escape from reality. Armed with just some food and a sleeping bag, you’re free from rules, away from other people, and able to enjoy the back-to-basics experience. One wild camper, Phoebe Smith, told the BBC: “The act of sleeping when everybody else has gone home – when you notice the wildlife and the stars – is one of the best things in life.”

But for those who still want some home comforts, a campsite is a more suitable place to pitch your tent. Here you have facilities such as washrooms, a shop and maybe even a restaurant. And for the most luxurious camping experience, you could try glamping. In the UK, camping – and caravanning – has always been popular. One survey by Visit Britain found around 4.38 million people go camping in Britain every year.

More recently, sales of camping gear have jumped as more people have opted for a staycation within the UK due to travel restrictions caused by the coronavirus pandemic. One camping retailer, Halfords, reported a surge in demand for products such as stoves, cool boxes and camping chairs. With the addition of inflatable mattresses and pillows, powerful torches and lamps to light up your tent and a better selection of easy-to-cook food, you can almost guarantee a comfortable and enjoyable camping expedition. The only thing you can’t guarantee, in the UK at least, is good weather! So maybe it’s time to slum it and give camping a try.

vocabulary.entry: slum it /slʌm ɪt/ 将就一下；凑活过
vocabulary.example: We don't have a hotel room, so we'll have to slum it in the tent for the night.
vocabulary.translation: 我们没有订到酒店房间，今晚只能在帐篷里将就一下了。

sentences.english: When you go on holiday, where do you like to stay?
sentences.chinese: 度假时，你喜欢住在哪里？

sentences.english: Do you like the luxury of a five-star hotel, the convenience of a self-catering apartment or do you prefer the freedom of sleeping under canvas?
sentences.chinese: 是偏爱五星级酒店的奢华、自助公寓的便利，还是更向往睡在帐篷里的无拘无束？

sentences.english: If you haven’t tried the latter, maybe you should join the increasing number of people who are enjoying the simple pleasures of camping.
sentences.chinese: 如果你还没试过最后一种，或许你应该像越来越多的人一样，去体验露营带来的简单乐趣。

sentences.english: By grabbing your tent, and some additional accessories, it’s easy to head off to the countryside and enjoy a night or two under the stars.
sentences.chinese: 带上帐篷和一些附加装备，很容易就可以前往郊外，在星空下度过一两晚。

sentences.english: Many campers are ditching the trappings of their modern, hectic life to do this, encouraged by experts who say a few peaceful nights in the middle of nowhere might be a good way to unwind and improve our sleep patterns and well-being.
sentences.chinese: 许多露营爱好者都会抛开现代快节奏生活的繁琐羁绊，选择这样的休闲方式。专家也表示，在偏远宁静的地方度过几个平和的夜晚，或许是放松身心、改善睡眠规律与身心健康的好办法。

sentences.english: It is also, of course, a good low-budget holiday option.
sentences.chinese: 当然，这也是一种低成本的度假选择。

sentences.english: For the adventurous, wild camping is the ultimate escape from reality.
sentences.chinese: 对于热爱冒险的人来说，野外露营是逃离现实的终极方式。

sentences.english: Armed with just some food and a sleeping bag, you’re free from rules, away from other people, and able to enjoy the back-to-basics experience.
sentences.chinese: 只带上些许食物和一个睡袋，你就能摆脱规则，远离人群，享受这种回归本真的体验。

sentences.english: One wild camper, Phoebe Smith, told the BBC: “The act of sleeping when everybody else has gone home – when you notice the wildlife and the stars – is one of the best things in life.”
sentences.chinese: 野外露营爱好者菲比·史密斯在接受BBC采访时说：“当所有人都已归家，你却在户外入眠——留意着周围的野生动物和满天繁星，这是生活中最美好的事情之一。”

sentences.english: But for those who still want some home comforts, a campsite is a more suitable place to pitch your tent.
sentences.chinese: 但对于那些仍想保留一些居家舒适的人来说，露营地会是更适合搭帐篷的地方。

sentences.english: Here you have facilities such as washrooms, a shop and maybe even a restaurant.
sentences.chinese: 这里有洗手间、小卖部，甚至可能有餐厅之类的设施。

sentences.english: And for the most luxurious camping experience, you could try glamping.
sentences.chinese: 而如果想体验最奢华的露营，你可以试试“精致露营”。

sentences.english: In the UK, camping – and caravanning – has always been popular.
sentences.chinese: 在英国，露营以及房车旅行向来十分受欢迎。

sentences.english: One survey by Visit Britain found around 4.38 million people go camping in Britain every year.
sentences.chinese: 英国旅游局的一项调查显示，每年约有438万人会在英国本土露营。

sentences.english: More recently, sales of camping gear have jumped as more people have opted for a staycation within the UK due to travel restrictions caused by the coronavirus pandemic.
sentences.chinese: 近年来，受新冠疫情引发的旅行限制影响，更多人选择在英国境内度假，露营装备的销量也随之猛增。

sentences.english: One camping retailer, Halfords, reported a surge in demand for products such as stoves, cool boxes and camping chairs.
sentences.chinese: 露营用品零售商哈福德公司报告称，炉具、冷藏箱和露营椅这类产品的需求激增。

sentences.english: With the addition of inflatable mattresses and pillows, powerful torches and lamps to light up your tent and a better selection of easy-to-cook food, you can almost guarantee a comfortable and enjoyable camping expedition.
sentences.chinese: 有了充气床垫和枕头、能照亮帐篷的强光手电筒与灯具，再加上种类更丰富的易于烹饪的食材，你几乎能确保拥有一次舒适愉悦的露营之旅。

sentences.english: The only thing you can’t guarantee, in the UK at least, is good weather!
sentences.chinese: 不过有一件事是无法保证的——至少在英国是这样——那就是晴朗的好天气！

sentences.english: So maybe it’s time to slum it and give camping a try.
sentences.chinese: 所以，或许是时候放下精致，去体验一次露营了。

title: Why are cat videos so popular
titleChinese: 我们为什么爱看猫咪视频？
paragraphs: We’ve all been there. One minute you’re searching for something serious, like a recipe for dinner, or something for work, and the next you’ve been sucked in by endless videos of cats doing funny things after seeing a catchy title in your suggested videos column. They’re compelling, engrossing and captivating, and you can end up spending hours watching kittens make funny noises or mistiming jumps. But why do these videos so often end up going viral? What makes them so enthralling? And why are they more popular than dog videos?

First, let’s talk about stereotypes. When many of us think about dogs, we imagine them rolling over onto their backs, tongues hanging out, or making a mess. They seem trusting and innocent – and they do silly things. Cats, on the other hand, seem somewhat more refined and independent. There’s a reason we have an expression ‘cool cat’. In short, cats seem more serious – and savvy. If we can get one over on a cat and make them do something like get in a box that slides down a hill, it’s comical. But with a dog, it’s not as funny because they trust you – and it’s easier. Tricking a cat, due to their wiliness, has more payoff.

The internet is filled with videos of cats making funny faces or reacting strangely. But why are they so funny? Well, simply – it’s unexpected. If you saw a cat walking down the street coolly or observing and preparing to attack a mouse, it wouldn’t be funny. But if that cat was walking sideways, wearing a silly costume, or becoming best friends with the mouse, suddenly we might start to laugh. Watching a cat that is normally majestic walk clunkily or pull a bizarre face is hilarious because it’s not something we would normally associate with that animal. It’s like watching someone who is normally very serious get the giggles. In some ways, we’re all laughing at their fall from grace.

So the next time you see one of those many memes of cats in awkward situations or videos that make you chuckle, try to remember why it’s so funny. And spare a thought for all those dogs that are trying to entertain us too.

vocabulary.entry: suck in /sʌk ɪn/ 吸引住；使卷入
vocabulary.example: The audience was sucked in by the actor's brilliant performance.
vocabulary.translation: 观众被这位演员的精彩表演吸引住了。

vocabulary.entry: catchy /ˈkætʃi/ adj. 朗朗上口的；吸引人的
vocabulary.example: The song has a catchy melody that everyone can hum.
vocabulary.translation: 这首歌的旋律朗朗上口，每个人都能跟着哼唱。

vocabulary.entry: compelling /kəmˈpelɪŋ/ adj. 引人入胜的；令人信服的
vocabulary.example: The novel tells a compelling story about love and betrayal.
vocabulary.translation: 这本小说讲述了一个关于爱与背叛的引人入胜的故事。

vocabulary.entry: engrossing /ɪnˈɡrəʊsɪŋ/ adj. 非常吸引人的；让人全神贯注的
vocabulary.example: It was an engrossing book that I couldn't put down.
vocabulary.translation: 这是一本非常吸引人的书，我简直爱不释手。

vocabulary.entry: captivating /ˈkæptɪveɪtɪŋ/ adj. 迷人的；有吸引力的
vocabulary.example: The singer has a captivating voice that won her many fans.
vocabulary.translation: 这位歌手有着迷人的嗓音，为她赢得了许多粉丝。

vocabulary.entry: viral /ˈvaɪrəl/ adj. （视频、信息等）病毒式传播的
vocabulary.example: The funny video went viral on social media within hours.
vocabulary.translation: 这个搞笑视频几小时内就在社交媒体上病毒式传播开来。

vocabulary.entry: enthralling /ɪnˈθrɔːlɪŋ/ adj. 使人着迷的；令人陶醉的
vocabulary.example: The magician gave an enthralling performance at the party.
vocabulary.translation: 这位魔术师在派对上献上了一场令人着迷的表演。

vocabulary.entry: stereotype /ˈsteriətaɪp/ n. 刻板印象；固有观念
vocabulary.example: There's a common stereotype that cats are not as loyal as dogs.
vocabulary.translation: 有一种常见的刻板印象认为猫不如狗忠诚。

vocabulary.entry: refined /rɪˈfaɪnd/ adj. 举止优雅的；精致的
vocabulary.example: She has a refined taste in art and literature.
vocabulary.translation: 她在艺术和文学方面有着高雅的品味。

vocabulary.entry: savvy /ˈsævi/ adj. 精明的；机智的
vocabulary.example: He is a savvy businessman who knows how to seize opportunities.
vocabulary.translation: 他是个精明的商人，懂得如何抓住机遇。

vocabulary.entry: cool cat /kuːl kæt/ 冷静时髦的人；淡定从容的人
vocabulary.example: He's a real cool cat who never gets flustered in emergencies.
vocabulary.translation: 他是个十足的淡定先生，在紧急情况下从不慌乱。

vocabulary.entry: get one over on /ɡet wʌn ˈəʊvə(r) ɒn/ 捉弄；占上风
vocabulary.example: She tried to get one over on her brother by hiding his game console.
vocabulary.translation: 她想捉弄一下弟弟，就把他的游戏机藏了起来。

vocabulary.entry: comical /ˈkɒmɪkl/ adj. 滑稽的；好笑的
vocabulary.example: The clown's comical gestures made the children laugh loudly.
vocabulary.translation: 小丑滑稽的动作让孩子们哈哈大笑。

vocabulary.entry: wiliness /ˈwaɪlinəs/ n. 狡猾；机灵
vocabulary.example: The fox's wiliness helps it escape from predators easily.
vocabulary.translation: 狐狸的狡猾让它能轻易摆脱捕食者的追捕。

vocabulary.entry: payoff /ˈpeɪɒf/ n. 回报；收益
vocabulary.example: All the hard work finally got a big payoff when the project succeeded.
vocabulary.translation: 项目成功后，所有的努力终于得到了丰厚的回报。

vocabulary.entry: unexpected /ˌʌnɪkˈspektɪd/ adj. 出乎意料的；意外的
vocabulary.example: We received an unexpected visit from our old friend last night.
vocabulary.translation: 昨晚我们的老朋友突然来访，让我们很意外。

vocabulary.entry: majestic /məˈdʒestɪk/ adj. 雄伟的；庄严的；高贵的
vocabulary.example: The eagle flew in a majestic manner above the mountains.
vocabulary.translation: 老鹰在山峦上方庄严地翱翔。

vocabulary.entry: clunkily /ˈklʌŋkɪli/ adv. 笨拙地；哐啷哐啷地
vocabulary.example: The old machine clunkily started up after several attempts.
vocabulary.translation: 这台旧机器尝试了好几次才哐啷哐啷地启动起来。

vocabulary.entry: bizarre /bɪˈzɑː(r)/ adj. 离奇的；古怪的
vocabulary.example: She had a bizarre dream about flying elephants last night.
vocabulary.translation: 她昨晚做了个离奇的梦，梦里全是会飞的大象。

vocabulary.entry: associate with /əˈsəʊsieɪt wɪð/ 把……联系起来；与……交往
vocabulary.example: People often associate the smell of jasmine with summer nights.
vocabulary.translation: 人们常常把茉莉花香和夏夜联系在一起。

vocabulary.entry: fall from grace /fɔːl frəm ɡreɪs/ 失势；形象受损；失去人心
vocabulary.example: The famous actor's fall from grace shocked all his fans.
vocabulary.translation: 这位著名演员的形象崩塌让他所有的粉丝都感到震惊。

vocabulary.entry: giggle /ˈɡɪɡl/ n. 咯咯的笑声 v. 咯咯地笑
vocabulary.example: The girls burst into a giggle when they heard the joke.
vocabulary.translation: 女孩们听到这个笑话后突然咯咯地笑了起来。

vocabulary.entry: meme /miːm/ n. 表情包；网络梗
vocabulary.example: This funny cat meme has been shared millions of times online.
vocabulary.translation: 这个搞笑的猫咪表情包已经在网上被分享了数百万次。

vocabulary.entry: awkward /ˈɔːkwəd/ adj. 令人尴尬的；笨拙的
vocabulary.example: He felt awkward when he realized he had worn the wrong clothes to the party.
vocabulary.translation: 当他意识到自己穿错衣服去派对时，感到很尴尬。

vocabulary.entry: chuckle /ˈtʃʌkl/ v. 轻声笑；暗自笑

vocabulary.translation: 老人读到孩子们写的搞笑诗歌时，忍不住轻声笑了起来。

title: The different eras of houses in the UK
paragraphs: There are many different types of houses in the UK. You may see detached, semi-detached, terraced houses or even end-of-terrace houses on a typical street. You might see mansions in more affluent parts of town, or people residing in bungalows, preferring to live a life without stairs. Quaint cottages may dot the countryside, while heading to the cities you could see any number of types of flats, including houses turned into converted flats, studios and duplexes. But one thing you will notice is that many houses come from different eras, and asking a British person about their ideal home, many of them will have a specific period property in mind.

For some, it could be Victorian houses, which are often seen with bay windows, high ceilings, stained glass doors and coloured brickwork. During the Victorian era, a huge number of houses, particularly terraced, were built in towns and cities to accommodate vast numbers of workers who were moving from more rural areas.

Georgian architecture refers to houses built during the period of 1714 and 1830 during the reigns of four British monarchs, all called George. Usually houses with this architectural style have a more symmetrical theme, both internally and externally, with a small square garden in front. For those not into older properties, new builds from the 1990s onwards offer better insulation against the cold and newer electrics. And those who prefer less maintenance could always go with the open-plan or minimalist look of the modern era.

So whether it’s high ceilings, better insulation, brickwork, bungalows or square gardens, people in Britain have a wide variety of preferences when it comes to where they live. And their ideal home may just simply be a case of what style feels like home.

vocabulary.entry: detached /dɪˈtætʃt/ adj. （房屋）独立式的
vocabulary.example: They bought a large detached house in the suburbs.
vocabulary.translation: 他们在郊区买了一栋宽敞的独立式房屋。

vocabulary.entry: semi-detached /ˌsemi dɪˈtætʃt/ adj. （房屋）半独立式的
vocabulary.example: The semi-detached villa shares a wall with the neighbouring house.
vocabulary.translation: 这栋半独立式别墅和隔壁房子共用一堵墙。

vocabulary.entry: terraced /ˈterəst/ adj. （房屋）联排式的
vocabulary.example: Terraced houses are common in the city centre.
vocabulary.translation: 联排房屋在市中心很常见。

vocabulary.entry: end-of-terrace /ˌend əv ˈterəs/ adj. 联排端头房的
vocabulary.example: The end-of-terrace house has windows on three sides.
vocabulary.translation: 这套联排端头房三面都有窗户。

vocabulary.entry: mansion /ˈmænʃn/ n. 豪宅；公馆
vocabulary.example: A historic mansion stands at the top of the hill.
vocabulary.translation: 一座历史悠久的豪宅坐落在山顶。

vocabulary.entry: affluent /ˈæfluənt/ adj. 富裕的；富足的
vocabulary.example: The hotel is located in an affluent neighbourhood.
vocabulary.translation: 这家酒店位于一个富裕的街区。

vocabulary.entry: reside /rɪˈzaɪd/ v. 居住；定居
vocabulary.example: She resides in a quiet village in the countryside.
vocabulary.translation: 她住在乡下一个宁静的村庄里。

vocabulary.entry: bungalow /ˈbʌŋɡələʊ/ n. 平房；单层住宅
vocabulary.example: The elderly couple moved into a bungalow to avoid climbing stairs.
vocabulary.translation: 这对老年夫妇搬进了一间平房，这样就不用爬楼梯了。

vocabulary.entry: quaint /kweɪnt/ adj. 古雅的；别致的

title: How to stay focused
paragraphs: When you were at school, were you ever told to stop daydreaming and concentrate? It was easy for your mind to wander if you weren’t interested in what you were learning or if you had better things to think about. Staying focused can still be a challenge in adult life, but understanding how to do it, and knowing what is distracting you, can help.

Scientists have looked at what makes us procrastinate and found a number of ways to help us stay in the zone. One of the most obvious things is eliminating noise. Research by Science Focus magazine found silence is best for concentration, or a gentle background hum and coffee shop noise is great! It also found turning off notifications on your phone, or switching it off altogether, removes a major distraction and helps us focus on the task at hand.

Another possible cure for a short attention span is brain training. Psychologists and neuroscientists are increasingly interested in our ability to knuckle down and have looked at what we can change inside our head to make us concentrate. An article for BBC Future by Caroline Williams says that “Attention Researcher Nilli Lavie of University College London has found that making a task more visually demanding… takes up more processing power and leaves the brain nothing left to process distractions.” So, keeping your mind busy might be the answer.

There are more practical tips to keeping your mind focused. These include making a list or timetable of the tasks you have to do, finding a workspace where you’re not tempted to do other things, or chewing some gum! It’s possible the movement in your mouth occupies parts of the brain that might otherwise get distracted.

But according to Science Focus magazine, distraction isn’t all bad. “If we were always so focused that we never got distracted, we’d miss potential changes, such as threats, in our environment. Distraction is vital for survival.”

title: Are our early memories real
titleChinese: 我们早期的记忆是真的吗？
paragraphs: What’s the first thing you remember doing? It could be playing with your friends at school, or going to a birthday party and eating amazing cake. Most of us have a treasured early memory of our childhood, but can we really believe those vivid memories? Did those special moments really happen – or did we make them up?

It’s a strange concept to grasp, but according to research, about four out of 10 of us invent our first childhood memory. Rather than having experienced something, we could have fabricated a fake memory from videos or photos we’ve seen. We could have been influenced by a story recounted to us that spurs our minds on to adopt someone else’s memory as our own. What it means is that memories of our younger years, especially before the age of two, may be inaccurate, or entirely false.

But why don’t we have clear memories from that age? Well, our ability to retain memories from before the age of two isn’t great. While at that age we do have short-term memories, according to Catherine Loveday, an expert in autobiographical memory at the University of Westminster, the memories that infants make are not long-lasting. This is possibly due to the rapid creation of brain cells in our early years. Some scientists also believe that as we get older, our childhood memories fade and after the age of seven, we get some kind of ‘childhood amnesia’.

So why do we create fake memories? Some experts believe that there is a clear desire for a sense of self and having a cohesive story of our existence. Creating memories can fill in the gaps – giving us a more complete structure for our early lives. As we get older, we want to have a complete picture of our entire lives.

So, the next time someone says they have a clear memory from when they were one – or even before - just remember that while it could be true, there’s a chance they just invented it at some point in their lives.

vocabulary.entry: treasured /ˈtreʒəd/ adj. 珍贵的；宝贵的
vocabulary.example: She kept the treasured letter from her grandfather in a wooden box.
vocabulary.translation: 她把祖父寄来的珍贵信件放在一个木盒子里。

title: Should we fear maths
titleChinese: 我们有必要害怕数学吗？
paragraphs: How good are you at maths? Some people love the challenge of algebra or enjoy working out number puzzles such as Sudoko. Maths is all around us, from working out how to split the bill after a meal, to calculating your household bills. But many dread the moment when they have to deal with numbers and figures and feel a real sense of worry and confusion. It can seem daunting, but this ‘maths anxiety’ is perfectly normal, and you’re definitely not alone. And anyway, our worries and fears don’t necessarily reflect our ability.

The problem really starts in childhood, at school. Research has found that maths teachers who are nervous about teaching the subject can pass on their anxiety to the pupils, and girls may be more likely to be affected. The Programme for International Student Assessment found around 31% of 15 and 16-year-olds across 34 countries said they got very nervous doing maths problems, 33% said they got tense doing maths homework, and nearly 60% said they worried maths classes would be difficult. Shulamit Kahn, from Boston University’s Questrom School of Business, told the BBC she believes giving students, particularly girls, good role models “is critical, especially at a young age”. She thinks the key is to get people, especially women, who love teaching maths to younger children.

Writing for BBC Future, David Robson says “It’s not clear why maths arouses so much fear compared to geography. But the fact that there’s a right or wrong answer – there’s no room for bluffing – might make you more worried about underperforming.” And once we assume we’re not a ‘maths person’, we avoid solving things that we probably could do.

Psychologists have been trying to work out why mental arithmetic can bring us out in a sweat. That seed of fear may come from many sources, but some suggest that articulating your fears can loosen their hold on you, and encourage children to see a maths test as a challenge, not a threat. Ideally, we need to think positively about maths and give it a second chance.

title: The dangers of loud noise
paragraphs: Many of us love live music – listening to the singer belting out classics we love to sing along to. But while it can be lots of fun nodding our heads to the tunes booming out, it can also harm our hearing. Studies suggest that one in ten adults have had their hearing damaged by loud noises or music. So why is loud music damaging, and what can we do to prevent it from harming our ears?

Inside our ears, there are lots of tiny hair-like cells located in the cochlea. These cells are referred to as hair cells because very small bundles of stereocilia, which look like hairs under a microscope, sit on top of each cell. These groupings of stereocilia can be damaged when exposed to prolonged loud noises. Once damaged, these cells cannot respond to sound, and therefore we are left with noise-induced hearing loss – which can be permanent. It can also leave us with a constant ringing sound in our ears, which is known as tinnitus. So, what sounds are too loud?

Sound is measured in decibels. The maximum safe level of sound humans are thought to be able to withstand without potential damage is 80db. The bangs or booms of a firework display can reach 120db, the whirring mechanical sound of a food processor can be around 85db, and live music can be around 110db. If these sounds continue for a long period of time, it puts our unprotected ears at risk.

So what can we do to protect our ears? Firstly, when listening to music, especially while using your headphones or earphones, make sure you keep it at a sensible volume. Also, don’t get too close to speakers that are blaring out music. And, if you go to live concerts, why not take some earbuds with you? Finally, if you get a ringing sensation in your ears, it might be wise to speak to your doctor as soon as possible. Your hearing is important, but there are some steps you can take to be as safe as possible.
